newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian government short of re-election votes -poll.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian government short of re-election votes -poll.

text.p: The Brazilian government is a long way short of the majority it needs next week to pass a law that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for a second term, a newspaper said on Friday.

The Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper said a poll of federal congressmen found only 200 favoured the bill, 108 short of the 308 needed for approval, while 126 opposed it and 62 only wanted to allow future presidents the chance of a second term.
Another 75 congressmen said they had not decided which way to vote and 50 were not located or did not answer the poll.
The survey showed appproval of the re-election amendment may not be the foregone conclusion the government has claimed.
Brazil has banned re-election since becoming a republic in 1889 in reaction to the authoritarian colonial rule it saw under the Portuguese monarchy.
Next week's vote is considered the biggest political challenge faced so far by the two-year Cardoso administration.
Supporters of re-election argue that the continuity of a second Cardoso term would help ensure the long-term success of economic reforms that have slashed inflation.
Public support for the government's Real Plan to stabilise the economy would make Cardoso a hard candidate to beat in the 1998 presidential elections, analysts say.

As a constitutionl amendment, the re-election bill needs three-fifths majorities in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate. The government hopes to put the legislation to a vote in a lower house committee on Tuesday, followed the next day by a first vote in the full Chamber of Deputies.
Deputy Jose Anibal, the lower house leader of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party, said he expected 330 deputies to vote in favour of allowing Cardoso to stand again.

"The poll has only one significant finding -- that 126 deputies are against re-election. Those who were undecided, in favour only for future presidents or not included, give us enough room to make up the 330," Anibal said.

A government source in Congress said deputies who declared themselves undecided or in favour of re-election only for future presidents would be the subject of intense lobbying by party leaders between now and Wednesday.
"There's going to be a lot of talking," he said.
